title: Your Post-Close Checklist: Insurance, Utilities & Handoff to Operations

slides.title: Write down everything the closing team learned before the launch team needs it
slides.subtitle: Lesson PA.12. Your Post-Close Checklist: Insurance, Utilities & Handoff to Operations
meta: Education only. Not legal, tax, or insurance advice.
slides.notes:
You own the house. This lesson turns it into something that's ready to become a rental.

After this lesson you can confirm you have the right insurance, move every utility and account into your control, and finish the safety work before anyone takes a photo.

The main output is a dated operations handoff packet. It tells the launch team everything the closing team learned, including what's still open. Nothing should fall between the two.

We'll follow Maya and Chris through the first 45 days at Cedar Ridge. The timeline and the carrying costs are assumptions built on the canonical figures. None of this is legal, tax, or insurance advice. Your insurer, licensing office, and CPA confirm the parts that depend on your address and your policy.

slides.title: The closing team and the launch team rarely talk, so a written packet has to carry the knowledge

left.head: The closing team
left.note: Knows what's wrong with the house.
items: Agent, lender, inspector, title company, attorney
The inspector knows the dock railing is loose
The seller named the septic company at the walkthrough

right.head: The launch team
items: Insurer, cleaner, handyman, furnishing help, maybe a co-host
Sam's OP.1 to OP.5 cover the listing and software
The cleaner and co-host never heard any of it

box.label: The handoff packet
box.text: Every open item gets an owner and a date. You may be both teams on your first property. Write the packet anyway.

slides.notes:
Up to now, your team was the closing team. Agent, lender, inspector, title company, attorney.

Now your team is the launch team. Insurer, cleaner, handyman, furnishing help, and maybe a co-host. Sam's OP.1 to OP.5 cover the listing and the software.

These two teams rarely talk to each other. The inspector knows the dock railing is loose. The cleaner doesn't. The seller told you the septic company's name at the walkthrough. Your co-host will never hear it unless you write it down.

The handoff packet is how the first team's knowledge reaches the second. Every open item gets an owner and a date.

On your first property, you're probably both teams. Write the packet anyway. The version of you who's answering a guest at 11 p.m. in February needs it.

slides.title: Read your policy as the operator, checking nine items the lender never asked about
items: Named insured matches your PA.10 decision
Effective date is the closing date or earlier
Covers short-term rental to paying guests, in writing
Liability limit per occurrence, including dock, water, and watercraft
Deductibles: all-perils, plus any wind, hail, or water deductible
Exclusions: slow leaks, mold, pools and hot tubs, 'business' use
Loss of rental income: when it pays, how it's calculated, for how long
Flood: your FEMA zone from PA.9 and whether you have a policy
Conditions: proof of railing and alarms sent, and confirmed in writing
slides.notes:
You bound a policy before closing, because the lender required it. Now read it as the operator. The lender cared that the house was insured. You care whether a guest injury, a burst pipe, or a month without bookings is covered.

Pull the declarations page and the policy form. Check these nine items.

The named insured has to match your PA.10 decision. The effective date has to be the closing date or earlier, because any gap is uninsured time. A standard homeowners policy may exclude business use, so get the insurer's answer on rental use in writing.

Check the liability limit, especially for the dock and the water. Note the deductibles. Read the exclusions. Check loss-of-rental-income coverage: when it pays, how it calculates lost income, and for how long.

And the conditions. PA.9's insurer wanted the railing and alarms done within 30 days. Send proof and get written confirmation.

slides.title: AirCover is a backup on some Airbnb claims, so your own policy carries the full load

left.head: What Airbnb says AirCover includes
items: Host damage protection and host liability insurance
Screening and a safety line
Protection while you're hosting an Airbnb stay

right.head: What Airbnb says it isn't
items: Host damage protection isn't an insurance policy
Not all damage is included
Not a substitute for your own insurance
A Vrbo or direct booking isn't an Airbnb stay

box.label: Flood has a waiting period
box.text: The NFIP generally has a 30-day wait, with exceptions such as buying when you make, increase, extend, or renew a mortgage. If you skipped flood at closing, the clock may start the day you buy.

slides.notes:
Now the platform. Airbnb's AirCover for Hosts includes host damage protection and host liability insurance, along with screening and a safety line.

Airbnb also says host damage protection isn't an insurance policy, and not all damage is included. It says AirCover isn't a substitute for your own insurance, and suggests talking to your insurer about overlap.

Airbnb describes AirCover as protection while you're hosting an Airbnb stay. A guest who books on Vrbo, or on your direct site from OP.3, isn't an Airbnb stay. Your own policy has to carry the whole load. Treat AirCover as a backup that may help on some Airbnb claims.

One more on flood. FEMA says most homeowners insurance doesn't cover flood. The NFIP generally has a 30-day waiting period, with exceptions, including buying when you make or renew a mortgage. If you skipped flood at closing, the clock may start the day you buy.

slides.title: Move every utility and account into your name within the first week
columns: What to set up at Cedar Ridge
rows: Autopay. A propane delivery schedule so the tank never runs dry mid-stay.
No bill. Note the shutoff, pump, pressure tank, and when the UV lamp is due.
Schedule the inspection and pumping program budgeted in PA.9.
Pickup day, bin size, whether the hauler serves rentals, who brings bins out.
Fastest reliable service. Test real speed in the bedrooms. Router out of guest reach.
A unique code for each stay and each vendor. Remove the seller's codes.
Follow Airbnb's device rules. Remove any indoor camera the seller left.
Forwarding or a local box. Permit renewals and tax notices arrive by mail.
Confirm who plows a private road, and when. Contract your own if needed.
slides.caption: Use the PA.11 walkthrough meter readings so the seller's final bills and your first bills split cleanly.
slides.notes:
Transfer every account into your name, or your entity's name, within the first week. Use the meter readings you took at the PA.11 walkthrough so the bills split cleanly.

Here's the list for a house like Cedar Ridge.

Electric and propane on autopay, with a propane delivery schedule. The well has no water bill, but it has a pump, a pressure tank, and the UV system the seller installed under the PA.9 amendment. Write down where the shutoff is and when the lamp is due. Schedule the septic program you budgeted.

Eight guests make more trash than a family. Confirm pickup day, bin size, and whether the hauler serves rentals.

Guests who work remotely will test the internet. Test real speed in the bedrooms, not just next to the router, and put the router where guests can't unplug it.

Set up the lock, mail, and snow plowing. We'll cover cameras next.

slides.title: Airbnb bans indoor cameras, even switched off, and requires disclosure of outdoor ones

left.head: Allowed, with rules
items: Smart home devices, with disclosure encouraged
Outdoor cameras, disclosed with general location before booking
Noise decibel monitors in common areas only, disclosed

right.head: Not allowed
items: Cameras that monitor indoor spaces, even if they're off
If the seller left an indoor camera, remove it

box.label: Credentials
box.text: Every login goes in a password manager with shared access. Don't email or text credentials. Turn on two-factor sign-in for utility, internet, lock, and platform accounts.

slides.notes:
Devices come with platform rules, so check them before you install anything.

Airbnb allows smart home devices and encourages you to disclose them. Outdoor cameras must be disclosed, with their general location, before booking. Noise decibel monitors are allowed only in common areas, and must be disclosed.

Airbnb doesn't allow cameras that monitor indoor spaces, even if they're turned off. If the seller left one, take it down.

Now credentials. Put every login in a password manager, with shared access for anyone who needs it. Don't email credentials or send them by text. The CFPB's closing-scam guidance warns that email isn't a secure way to send financial information. Treat account logins the same way.

Turn on two-factor sign-in for the utility, internet, lock, and platform accounts. It takes an afternoon and closes an easy door.

slides.title: Build the vendor list now, while nothing is broken
items: Cleaner ($150 a turnover): intro visit before OP.8
Handyman or inspection retainer ($150 a month): full walk, incl. dock, septic, well
Septic, well and water treatment, HVAC, and pest services from PA.9
Emergency plumber and electrician for nights and weekends
Plow service and trash hauler
Backup cleaner or local co-host for a missed clean (OP.7)
Local licensing office and lodging tax contact

box.label: Vendor access
box.text: Give each vendor their own lock code, and delete it when the job ends. Record who has a physical key, if anyone does.

slides.notes:
Your vendor list is the difference between a two-hour fix and a cancelled stay. Build it now, while you're calm.

The cleaner is on the canonical budget at $150 a turnover. Set up an intro visit before OP.8 builds the cleaning SOP.

The on-call handyman or inspection retainer is on the budget at $150 a month. Walk them through the whole house, including the dock and the septic and well equipment.

Most of the specialists came out of PA.9: septic, well and water treatment, HVAC, and pest. Add an emergency plumber and electrician who answer nights and weekends. Add the plow service and the trash hauler.

Have one backup name for a missed clean. OP.7 covers the bigger choice between a cleaner, a co-host, or a property manager.

Give each vendor their own lock code and delete it when the job ends.

slides.title: File the permit and lodging tax registration before the first stay

nodes.d: Cedar Ridge's permit didn't transfer, so they apply as new owners.
Don't publish first if local rules require the permit.
Airbnb's laws and regulations section. Sam's OP.1 builds the listing.
Separate from the permit. Lesson 3.3 covers collection.

box.label: Your SR.1 checklist
box.text: Records the exact local rule and the date you checked it. Bring the permit number and the exact holder name to Sam's OP.1.

slides.notes:
Diligence told you whether this address can run a rental. Now you file.

For Cedar Ridge, PA.9 found the seller's permit doesn't transfer. So Maya and Chris apply as new owners. Don't publish a listing before the permit is issued if the local rules require the permit first. Your SR.1 checklist records the exact rule and when you checked it.

When the permit number comes back, Airbnb has a field for it. It sits under the listing's policies and rules, in the laws and regulations section. Sam's OP.1 shows listing setup across platforms. Bring the permit number and the exact holder name to that lesson.

Lodging and occupancy tax registration is separate from the permit. Register with the state or local tax agency before your first stay. Airbnb's guidance says hosts should look up local taxes and business license rules. Part One lesson 3.3 walks through channel-by-channel collection.

slides.title: Finish the safety work before photos, because photos set what guests expect
items: Smoke and CO detectors: disclosed, working, tested regularly (Airbnb)
CO alarms on every level, outside sleeping areas (CPSC)
At least one fire extinguisher (CPSC)
TVs and furniture anchored to the wall (CPSC)
Pool and spa drain covers that meet federal standards (CPSC)
No blocked exits, exposed wiring, mold, pests, or contaminated water (Airbnb)
Instructions for features that could injure if misused: dock, lake, stairs

box.label: Cedar Ridge sign-off
box.text: One page: each item, who checked it, the date, and a photo. Dock railing, lower-level alarms, HVAC service, a clean well retest, and a clear exit from every bedroom.

slides.notes:
Don't photograph a house you haven't finished fixing. Photos lock in what guests expect, and a listing can't promise a deck that isn't safe yet.

Start with the PA.9 punch list. Then walk the house against Airbnb's safety requirements. Airbnb says hosts must disclose whether smoke and CO detectors are present, and if they are, they must work and be tested. Its hazard list includes blocked exits, exposed wiring, poorly maintained hot tubs or furnaces, contaminated water, mold, and pests. Airbnb says it may require proof that issues are fixed before a listing can take reservations.

The CPSC's vacation rental tips add a few practical items: CO alarms on every level, an extinguisher, anchored furniture, and drain covers.

OP.6 builds these into the furnishing plan. Here, you just need the structural and system items done, on a one-page sign-off.

slides.title: Forty-five days without guests cost Maya and Chris $4,510.50 in carrying costs
slides.side: Maya and Chris closed on day 0 and plan to launch on about day 45.

side_box.label: The number to watch
side_box.text: If the permit takes longer, each extra month costs another $3,007.

slides.notes:
Maya and Chris closed on day 0. They plan to launch on about day 45. That's an assumption. Here's what those 45 days cost before a single booking.

Carrying costs keep running with no revenue. Monthly PITIA on the DSCR loan is $2,557. Utilities, internet, and trash are $450 a month. That's $3,007 a month.

For 45 days, that's $3,007 times 1.5, or $4,510.50.

The number to watch is the permit. If it takes longer than planned, each extra month costs another $3,007. That's why the permit application goes in on day 2, not after the furniture arrives.

[Recording note: Preston can add a real example here if he has one.]

slides.title: Between closing and the first guest, $39,465.50 leaves Maya and Chris's accounts
rows: PA.9 repairs paid by the buyers
**Cash out between closing and first guest**

box.label: What's left
box.text: The $142,688 total cash in already includes the $32,000 furnishing. So: $210,000 - $142,688 - $2,955 - $4,510.50 = $59,846.50 left. The 45-day carry draws on the six-month PITIA reserve set aside in PA.8.

slides.notes:
Now the one-time costs. The post-close repairs from PA.9 total $2,955. That's the dock railing, the alarms, and the HVAC service. The seller handled the septic and well work before closing.

Furnishing is budgeted at $32,000. OP.6 covers how to spend it.

Add the $4,510.50 carry, and $39,465.50 goes out between closing and the first guest.

Careful with the savings math. The canonical total cash in of $142,688 already includes the $32,000 furnishing. So from their $210,000 of liquid savings, subtract $142,688, the $2,955, and the $4,510.50. That leaves $59,846.50.

In PA.8 they set aside six months of PITIA, which is $15,342, plus a $30,000 emergency fund and a weak-case cushion, all from that money. The 45-day carry draws on the PITIA reserve.

slides.notes:
Here's their day-by-day plan. It's an assumption, but the shape is what I'd copy.

Day 0, the day of closing, Maya resets the lock codes, removes the seller's device accounts, and takes photos and meter readings.

In the first few days, Chris moves the utilities and sets up autopay. Maya confirms the insurance declarations and the conditions. On day 2, Chris files the permit application and registers for lodging tax.

The handyman and vendors handle the railing, alarms, and HVAC between days 3 and 10. The lab retests the well on day 12. Furnishing runs from day 10 to 30.

The safety sign-off walk is day 30. Photos come after, on day 32. The listing and software get built from day 30 to 44, using Sam's OP.1 to OP.5.

Day 45 is the first guest, if the permit is issued. Notice every row has a name.

Names exactly as on deed, insurance, permit
Water main, well pump, UV, septic lid, panel, propane, HVAC filter size
Carrier, policy number, named insured, limits, deductibles, claim phone, renewal
Zone, policy yes/no, carrier, effective date
Permit number, holder, expiry; lodging tax account, filing frequency

slides.caption: The full packet in PA.12.8 also has a Source column for every field.
slides.notes:
Here's the exercise: build the operations handoff packet and date it. Update the date every time you change it.

The full packet has 21 fields. I've split it across two slides. This first half is the property itself.

The packet date and version. The property facts, including the permitted guest capacity from PA.9. The title owner and operator, spelled exactly as on the deed, the insurance, and the permit. A floor plan showing exits, shutoffs, the panel, and alarms. Where every shutoff and system lives, down to the HVAC filter size.

Then insurance, flood, permits and tax, utilities, and internet.

In the lesson each field also has a source column, like the declarations page or the inspector's report. Fill that in too. When a field changes, you'll know where to check.

slides.title: Finish the packet with the people, schedules, reserves, and every open issue
rows: Lock model, how codes are issued, vendor codes list, key holders
Outdoor cameras and noise monitor: location, disclosed; thermostat
Location in password manager; who has access
Cleaner, backup, handyman, septic, well, HVAC, plumber, electrician, pest, plow, trash, co-host
Room-by-room furniture and supplies (filled in OP.6)
Septic, well test, UV lamp, HVAC, alarm tests, roof check, gutters
Fire, CO, leak, power loss, dock injury, weather; who calls whom
Roof, HVAC, water heater, appliances, septic and well invoices
Roof sinking fund, capital reserve, operating reserve
Every row from the PA.11 log, with owner and due date
slides.notes:
The second half is about people and time.

Access and devices, including where the outdoor cameras and noise monitor sit and whether they're disclosed. Where the credentials live. Keep the credentials themselves in the password manager, not in the packet.

The contact list from the vendor slide. The inventory, which OP.6 fills in. A maintenance schedule built from the PA.9 findings: septic, well test, UV lamp, HVAC, alarm tests, the roof, and the gutters.

An emergency plan. OP.8 turns it into an SOP. The safety sign-off. Warranties and records. The budget reserves from the PA.9 rerun, including the roof sinking fund.

And last, open issues. Every row from your PA.11 unresolved items log goes here, with its owner and due date. Store the packet where your cleaner, handyman, and co-host can read it.

slides.title: Nothing goes live until the insurance, permit, and safety rows say done

gates.q: Does the insurance row say done?
gates.sub: Rental use, limits, conditions confirmed in writing.

gates.q: Does the permit row say done?
gates.sub: Issued, if local rules require it before listing.

gates.q: Does the safety sign-off row say done?
Does every open issue have one owner and one due date?
gates.no: Assign one name and one date

slides.end: All yes: go live. Update the packet version whenever a vendor, code, or policy changes.
slides.notes:
The packet has three rules. I've turned them into gates you check before you publish anything.

The first rule is that nothing goes live until three rows say done. Insurance, with rental use and conditions confirmed in writing. The permit, if your local rules require it before listing. And the safety sign-off, signed and dated.

The second rule is that every open issue has one owner and one due date. 'We' is not an owner. If a row says 'we,' it belongs to nobody.

The third rule is about upkeep. Update the packet version whenever a vendor, a code, or a policy changes. A packet from three months ago with the old cleaner's number is worse than useless at 11 p.m.

slides.title: Five parties confirm the coverage, permit, tax, safety, and records before launch
rows: Rental use, liability limits, deductibles, exclusions, loss of income, conditions met, flood, named insured
Permit issuance, holder's name, occupancy limit, whether you can list before issuance
Lodging tax registration and filing frequency
The safety and system items on your sign-off
Records and accounts to set up now, and the date the property is ready and available to rent (PA.5 timing)
slides.notes:
Here's who confirms what after closing.

Your insurer confirms rental-use coverage, the liability limits, deductibles, exclusions, loss-of-income terms, that the conditions are met, flood coverage, and the named insured. Get it in writing.

The local licensing office confirms the permit, whose name it's in, the occupancy limit, and whether you can list before it's issued.

The state or local tax agency confirms your lodging tax registration and how often you file.

A licensed electrician, septic inspector, or certified water lab confirms the safety and system items on your sign-off, as needed.

And your CPA confirms the bookkeeping records and accounts to set up now. The CPA also confirms the date the property is ready and available to rent. That date affects depreciation timing in Sam's PA.5, so don't guess it.

slides.notes:
The house is insured, connected, safe, and documented. Next come Sam's operations demos. I won't re-teach them here. Here's what to bring to each one.

OP.1 and OP.2 show the listing build. Bring your permit number, your real guest capacity, and your safety disclosures.

OP.3 and OP.4 connect the lock, the messaging, and the software. Bring your device list and your access plan from the packet.

OP.5 sets rates. Bring the PA.9 revised baseline, so your pricing targets use the real cost structure. For Cedar Ridge that means the $3,820 of added annual costs, not the original PA.4 lines.

Then I pick up again in OP.6, where the $32,000 furnishing budget turns into a room-by-room plan.

slides.title: Lock down coverage, access, and the permit clock in your first week of ownership
items: Pull your declarations page and check the nine insurance items against it.

File the STR permit application, or confirm the date you will.

slides.next: Next: Sam's OP.1 Listing Creation Across Airbnb, VRBO & Booking.com. Bring your permit number, guest capacity, and safety disclosures. I pick up in OP.6 Furnishing & Interior Optimization.
slides.notes:
Four things this week. Each one takes under an hour.

First, pull your declarations page and check the nine items against it. Write down anything you need to ask the insurer.

Second, reset every lock code and remove the seller's accounts from each device.

Third, file the STR permit application. If you can't file yet, find out exactly what's missing and put the date on your calendar. Every extra month of waiting costs Cedar Ridge $3,007.

Fourth, start the handoff packet. Date it, fill in the property facts, and write the names exactly as they appear on the deed, the insurance, and the permit.

That closes Phase 1. Next is Sam's OP.1 Listing Creation. Bring your permit number, guest capacity, and safety disclosures. After Sam's OP.1 to OP.5, I pick up in OP.6 Furnishing & Interior Optimization.

slides.notes:
These are the sources behind this lesson.

Most of the platform rules come from Airbnb's own help center: what AirCover includes and doesn't, the safety requirements, the camera and device rules, where the permit number goes, and the host's responsibility for insurance, taxes, and permits.

The flood points come from FEMA and FloodSmart. The practical safety items come from the CPSC's vacation rental tips. The credentials point borrows from the CFPB's closing-scam guidance.

Each one was checked on September 25, 2026, through a search summary of the official page, because direct fetches were blocked. Airbnb updates its help articles often, so open them yourself before you set up your listing.

The Cedar Ridge figures come from the canonical example. The 45-day launch and the day plan are assumptions.
